title: FAR U3·W3 — Not-for-Profit Accounting (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — two net-asset buckets, not retained earnings

Not-for-profit entities (charities, foundations, private universities, many hospitals) follow FASB but with their own twists: equity is called net assets and split by donor restriction, and contributions are the defining transaction. The construction connection is real — MBG-style builders frequently work for nonprofits and faith-based developers — and FAR tests NFP every form.

Two classes of net assets

Under current standards, an NFP reports just two classes of net assets:

  • Net assets without donor restrictions — available for any purpose at the board's discretion.
  • Net assets with donor restrictions — limited by donors as to purpose or time (including permanently restricted endowments).

When a donor restriction is satisfied (the purpose is fulfilled or the time passes), the amount is reclassified from net assets with donor restrictions to net assets without donor restrictions — shown as a "net assets released from restrictions" line.

Contributions

A contribution is an unconditional, nonreciprocal transfer of assets. It is recognized as revenue at fair value when received or unconditionally promised (a pledge). Classify it by whether the donor imposed a restriction.

A conditional contribution — one with a barrier the NFP must overcome and a right of return if it does not — is not recognized until the condition is substantially met; cash received in advance is a refundable liability. Distinguish a condition (a barrier) from a restriction (a donor limit on use): a conditional gift is not yet revenue, while a restricted gift is revenue now, just in the restricted class.

Exchange versus contribution

An exchange transaction is reciprocal — the NFP provides commensurate value (tuition, a service fee) — and follows ASC 606 revenue recognition. A contribution is nonreciprocal. Many transactions are part-exchange, part-contribution (a $500 gala ticket for a $100 dinner has a $400 contribution element).

Statements and donated items

NFPs present a statement of financial position, a statement of activities, and a statement of cash flows; expenses are reported by function (program services vs supporting — management and general, and fundraising) and by nature. Donated services are recognized only if they create or enhance a nonfinancial asset, or require specialized skills the donor possesses and the NFP would otherwise buy. Donated materials are recognized at fair value.

Endowments and UPMIFA

An endowment is a fund meant to be invested with the principal preserved. A donor-restricted endowment (the donor requires principal be held permanently or for a term) sits in net assets with donor restrictions; a board-designated endowment — a quasi-endowment — is the board’s own earmarking of unrestricted funds and stays in net assets without donor restrictions, because a board can reverse its own designation. Most states’ UPMIFA statute governs spending: absent explicit donor terms, the original gift amount is classified as restricted and appreciation is restricted until appropriated for spending. An underwater endowment — fair value below the original gift — is still reported within net assets with donor restrictions, with the shortfall disclosed.

Promises to give and investment return

Unconditional promises to give collectible in future years are recorded at the present value of expected cash flows, with the discount accreted to contribution revenue over time, and reduced by an allowance for uncollectible pledges. Investment returns — interest, dividends, and realized and unrealized gains on endowment and other investments — are reported net of external and direct internal investment expenses and classified by the presence or absence of donor restrictions on the income. A donor may restrict the income of an endowment even when the principal is permanent, so the return can land in either net-asset class depending on the gift terms.

Required statements and functional expenses

Every NFP must present an analysis of expenses by both function and natural classification — historically a separate statement of functional expenses, now required of all NFPs in some form (statement, schedule, or notes). Functions divide into program services (the mission) and supporting services (management and general, fundraising, and membership development). Costs that benefit more than one function are allocated, and the methods are disclosed; the program-to-supporting ratio is a metric donors and watchdogs scrutinize. The core statements remain the statement of financial position, the statement of activities (showing the change in each net-asset class), and the statement of cash flows.

Liquidity, agency transactions, and contributed assets

ASU 2016-14 added a required liquidity and availability disclosure: qualitative information on how the NFP manages liquidity plus a quantitative measure of financial assets available within one year to meet general expenditures, since donor restrictions can lock up resources. An agency (pass-through) transaction — where the NFP receives assets to transfer to a specified third party — is not contribution revenue; the NFP records a liability to the ultimate beneficiary. A gift of a long-lived asset (or cash restricted to acquire one) may be released from restriction either when placed in service or over the asset’s useful life, depending on the NFP’s accounting policy.

Healthcare NFPs and the bottom line

Not-for-profit healthcare entities add wrinkles: they report a performance indicator (analogous to income from operations) on the statement of operations, present patient service revenue net of contractual adjustments with explicit and implicit price concessions, and recognize charity care as a disclosure only (no revenue) because payment was never expected. Across all NFPs the through-line is the same: equity is net assets viewed through the lens of donor intent, contributions — not retained earnings — drive the change in net assets, and the statements exist to show whether the organization honored the restrictions attached to the resources entrusted to it.

Split-interest gifts and special events

Two recurring NFP transactions round out the picture. A split-interest agreement — a charitable remainder trust or charitable gift annuity — gives the NFP a future interest while another beneficiary receives payments for a time; the NFP recognizes contribution revenue for the present value of its expected residual interest and a liability for amounts owed to the other beneficiary, remeasured as actuarial assumptions update. A special event such as a gala is split into its exchange and contribution elements: the fair value of the direct benefit to the attendee (the meal) is exchange revenue, and the excess paid is a contribution. Worked split: a $500 gala ticket where the dinner’s fair value is $90 yields $90 of exchange revenue and a $410 contribution — and it is the fair value received, not whether the attendee shows up, that fixes the split. The direct costs of the benefit may be netted against special-event revenue or shown as a cost of supporting services, with the policy disclosed. These mechanics reinforce the unit’s core test — separate what the donor gave freely from what they received in return, and recognize each under its own rule.

CMA bridge

The contribution-recognition logic mirrors ASC 606's control and condition concepts from FAR Unit 1, and the functional-expense split parallels the responsibility-center thinking from CMA month 3 — here the categories are program versus supporting services.

Practice and recap

  1. Report two net-asset classes: with and without donor restrictions.
  2. Recognize contributions at fair value when unconditional; reclassify when restrictions are met.
  3. Do not recognize conditional contributions until the barrier is overcome.
  4. Separate exchange transactions (ASC 606) from contributions; report expenses by function.

Recap: NFPs split net assets into with- and without-donor-restriction classes, recognize unconditional contributions at fair value now and reclassify on release, defer conditional gifts until the barrier is met, and report expenses by function.

flashcards.front: Two net-asset classes for an NFP
flashcards.back: Net assets without donor restrictions and net assets with donor restrictions.

flashcards.front: When is an unconditional contribution recognized?
flashcards.back: At fair value when received or unconditionally promised (pledged).
A condition is a barrier (gift not yet revenue); a restriction is a donor limit on use (revenue now, restricted class).

flashcards.front: How is a conditional contribution treated before the condition is met?
flashcards.back: Not recognized as revenue; advance cash is a refundable liability.

flashcards.front: What happens when a donor restriction is satisfied?
flashcards.back: Reclassify from net assets with donor restrictions to without (net assets released from restrictions).
Exchange is reciprocal (ASC 606); contribution is nonreciprocal.
Only if they create/enhance a nonfinancial asset or require specialized skills the NFP would otherwise purchase.
By function (program services vs supporting: management/general and fundraising) and by nature.

questions.q: How many net-asset classes does an NFP report under current standards?
questions.explain: Current standards use two classes: with and without donor restrictions.

questions.q: An unconditional pledge to donate is recognized:
choices: At fair value when the promise is made
questions.explain: Unconditional contributions, including pledges, are recognized at fair value when promised.

questions.q: A gift with a barrier the NFP must overcome and a right of return is:
choices: A conditional contribution — not recognized until the condition is met
questions.explain: A conditional contribution is deferred until the barrier is substantially met.

questions.q: When a purpose restriction is satisfied, the amount is:
choices: Reclassified from with-restriction to without-restriction net assets
questions.explain: Satisfying a restriction reclassifies net assets (net assets released from restrictions).

questions.q: Tuition charged by a private university is primarily:
questions.explain: Tuition is reciprocal value — an exchange transaction recognized under ASC 606.

questions.q: NFP expenses must be reported by:
questions.explain: NFPs report expenses by function and by nature.

questions.q: Donated services are recognized only when they:
choices: Create/enhance a nonfinancial asset or require specialized skills otherwise purchased
questions.explain: Donated services are recognized only under the create/enhance or specialized-skills criteria.
